pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of PLANT)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of plant, from Latin plantare (to plant, fix in the ground), formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Which thou plantedst not... how thou didst afflict the people, and cast them out.

Plantedst appears twice in the Authorized Version, and both times it names something thou didst NOT do. In Deuteronomy 6:11 Moses warns Israel of houses full of good things which thou filledst not, wells digged which thou diggedst not, and vineyards and olive trees which thou plantedst not — the whole verse a catalogue of unearned inheritance, warning against the forgetfulness that unearned plenty breeds. In Psalm 44:2 the sense inverts: there plantedst names what God did do for the fathers, driving out the heathen and plantedst them in the land, the very verb of Deuteronomy 6 now describing not Israel's false claim to have laboured but the LORD's own sovereign act of settling His people. Read together, the two occurrences frame the whole conquest of Canaan as gift rather than achievement: the vineyards Israel did not plant are the vineyards God plantedst by His own hand, and the danger named in Deuteronomy is precisely the temptation to forget which of those two plantedst is true. The archaic thou-form presses the address personally — this is not a general truth about nations but the LORD speaking to a covenant people who might otherwise credit their own labour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PLANT: to put into the ground for growth; to set; to fix or establish; here in the archaic second-person singular past, plantedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: PLANT, v.t. To put into the ground and cover, as seed for growth.
PLANT, v.t. To set in the earth for growth, as a tree, vine, or slip.
PLANT, v.t. To fix or set firmly; to establish; to settle, as a people in a land.
PLANTEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as filledst, diggedst.
In Deuteronomy 6:11 the word names the vineyards Israel did not plant but inherited; in Psalm 44:2 it names the LORD's own act of settling His people in the land.
scriptures: Deu 6:11
And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;
Psa 44:2
How thou didst drive out the heathen with thy hand, and plantedst them; how thou didst afflict the people, and cast them out.
corruption_summary: A moralistic reading turns Deuteronomy 6:11 into a lesson about gratitude in general, missing that the passage's whole warning concerns the specific danger of a redeemed people forgetting they were plantedst by grace and beginning to imagine themselves self-made.
corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic gloss on Deuteronomy 6 can flatten it into generic advice to count one's blessings, detached from the covenant context: this is Moses addressing a people about to enter a land of houses, wells, and vineyards they did not build, dig, or plant, warning that forgetting the true Planter breeds the self-satisfaction that leads straight to idolatry (the very next verses name that danger explicitly). The word plantedst is not decorative; it is the pivot on which the warning turns.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that plantedst names sovereign gift in both its occurrences — the vineyards Israel did not plant, and the people God did — and the right response to unearned plenty is remembrance of the Planter, not quiet reassignment of credit to oneself.
roots_summary: Plantedst occurs only twice, in Deuteronomy's warning against forgetting unearned inheritance and in Psalm 44's remembrance of the conquest as the LORD's own planting, the two verses together framing Canaan as gift rather than achievement.
roots_lines: Plantedst in Deuteronomy 6:11 names vineyards and olive trees Israel inherited without planting them.
The verse pairs plantedst with filledst and diggedst, a triple catalogue of unearned plenty.
Plantedst in Psalm 44:2 names God's own act of settling His people in the land He cleared for them.
The same verb that names Israel's false claim to labour also names the LORD's true labour on their behalf.
Deuteronomy 8, immediately following this theme, warns explicitly against saying 'my power hath gotten me this wealth.'
usage: Vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not — the danger of forgetting unearned inheritance.
Plantedst them — the LORD's own settling of His people in the land He gave them.
The same verb frames both Israel's temptation and God's true labour, a single word carrying two meanings.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of PLAY)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of play, from Old English plegan, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version; in this occurrence part of the fixed idiom 'played the harlot.'
biblical_def:
Thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown.

Playedst appears once in the Authorized Version, in Ezekiel's long oracle against Jerusalem under the figure of a bride turned adulteress. The word belongs to the fixed idiom played the harlot, the standing Old Testament figure for covenant unfaithfulness — Israel is not accused of a single sin but of a settled character, a trade taken up and continued. Ezekiel 16 traces the logic with unusual precision: the LORD found Jerusalem an abandoned infant, raised her, clothed her, entered covenant with her, and made her beautiful; and it is precisely that given beauty which becomes the occasion of her unfaithfulness — thou didst trust in thine own beauty. The renown that should have turned to gratitude toward the Giver instead turned inward, and inward trust in a gift became the platform from which Jerusalem playedst the harlot with every passer-by, spending covenant blessing on rival gods and rival nations. The verse names a pattern that runs throughout the prophets: unfaithfulness rarely begins with denial of the LORD's gifts but with quiet confidence in them, a beauty enjoyed apart from the One who gave it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PLAY: to sport; to trifle; in the idiom 'play the harlot,' to act unfaithfully; here in the archaic second-person singular past, playedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: PLAY, v.i. To sport; to frolic; to do something not as a serious occupation.
PLAY, v.i. In Scripture idiom, to play the harlot: to act the part of an unfaithful wife, figuratively of covenant unfaithfulness to God.
PLAYEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as trustedst.
In Ezekiel 16 the word describes Jerusalem's covenant unfaithfulness under the figure of harlotry.
The idiom 'played the harlot' recurs throughout the prophets as the standing figure for Israel's idolatry.
scriptures: But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown, and pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by; his it was.
corruption_summary: A reading that treats Ezekiel 16 as merely ancient shock rhetoric misses that the oracle diagnoses a precise spiritual mechanism — trust in a given beauty curdling into self-trust — that has nothing to do with the sexual bluntness of the imagery and everything to do with the ordinary temptation of any blessed people.
corruption_paragraphs: A squeamish handling of Ezekiel 16 can treat the whole chapter as an embarrassment to be summarized rather than read, losing the verse's actual diagnostic force: the harlotry does not begin with a foreign temptation arriving from outside but with an internal turn, thou didst trust in thine own beauty. The chapter names the mechanism by which gift becomes idol precisely so later readers can recognize it in themselves.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that playedst names a settled unfaithfulness that begins in misplaced trust, not a single act; the remedy the prophets everywhere hold out is not self-improvement but return to the Husband who gave the beauty in the first place.
roots_summary: Playedst occurs once, in Ezekiel's extended oracle tracing Jerusalem's unfaithfulness from a given beauty to a settled harlotry, the single occurrence anchoring the whole chapter's argument.
roots_lines: Playedst in Ezekiel 16:15 names the turn from trusting God's gift to trusting oneself.
The verse's own logic: renown given by God became occasion for playedst the harlot.
Ezekiel 16 opens with Jerusalem as an abandoned infant raised and beautified by the LORD.
The idiom 'play the harlot' recurs across Hosea, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel as the standing figure for idolatry.
The chapter closes with the promise of an everlasting covenant despite the unfaithfulness it exposes.
usage: Thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot — the mechanism of gift becoming idol.
Because of thy renown — the very blessing given by God became the occasion of unfaithfulness.
Pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by — settled character, not a single act.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of SHEW)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of shew (the Authorized Version's standard spelling of show), from Old English sceawian (to look at, behold), formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Shewedst signs and wonders upon Pharaoh... then thou shewedst me their doings.

Shewedst appears twice in the Authorized Version, in two prayers addressed directly to God concerning what He has already shewedst. Nehemiah 9:10 recalls the exodus plagues — signs and wonders shewedst upon Pharaoh — as the founding evidence of the LORD's power on Israel's behalf, cited in a long communal confession that moves from that founding mercy through centuries of Israel's unfaithfulness. Jeremiah 11:18 is more personal and darker: the prophet recounts that the LORD shewedst me their doings, the doings in question being a plot by his own townsmen of Anathoth to kill him for his preaching. Together the two occurrences frame shewedst as the verb of divine disclosure in two directions — outward, in the great public acts of redemption every generation must remember, and inward, in the private revealing of hidden danger to a single threatened servant. Both are gifts of the same kind: the LORD shewedst what could not otherwise be known, whether the plagues that broke Pharaoh's grip or the conspiracy that would have taken Jeremiah unawares.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SHEW (the AV spelling of show): to exhibit; to make visible; to make known; here in the archaic second-person singular past, shewedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: SHEW, v.t. To exhibit; to present to the view.
SHEW, v.t. To make known; to declare; to make clear by evidence or reasoning.
SHEW, v.t. To point out; to inform; to teach.
SHEWEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as knewest.
In Nehemiah 9:10 the word names the plagues shewedst upon Pharaoh; in Jeremiah 11:18 it names hidden doings disclosed to the threatened prophet.
scriptures: Neh 9:10

And shewedst signs and wonders upon Pharaoh, and on all his servants, and on all the people of his land: for thou knewest that they dealt proudly against them. So didst thou get thee a name, as it is this day.
And the LORD hath given me knowledge of it, and I know it: then thou shewedst me their doings.
corruption_summary: A generic reading of divine 'signs' as mere ancient spectacle misses that both occurrences of shewedst concern God disclosing what would otherwise remain hidden — Pharaoh's coming defeat, a prophet's coming danger — a category with plain contemporary force wherever providence reveals what could not have been known by ordinary means.
corruption_paragraphs: A rationalist handling of Nehemiah's plagues or Jeremiah's warning can treat both as folklore dressed as history, missing that the text presents shewedst in both cases as a specific, datable disclosure with real consequences — Pharaoh's household broken, a plot against Jeremiah's life exposed in time for him to escape it.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that shewedst in both verses names a mercy of disclosure, not decoration: the God who shewedst Pharaoh's plagues is the same God who shewedst Jeremiah his enemies' doings, and both mercies were given so that the recipients might act rightly with the knowledge given them.
roots_summary: Shewedst occurs twice, once in a national confession recalling the exodus plagues and once in a personal lament recalling a private disclosure to an endangered prophet, together spanning the public and private reach of divine revealing.
roots_lines: Shewedst in Nehemiah 9:10 names the plagues by which the LORD broke Pharaoh's grip on Israel.
That verse ties shewedst to the LORD getting Himself a name that endures 'as it is this day.'
Shewedst in Jeremiah 11:18 names a private disclosure of a murder plot against the prophet.
Jeremiah's own response follows immediately: he commits his cause to the LORD as a righteous judge.
The two occurrences together frame shewedst as covering both national history and personal providence.
usage: Shewedst signs and wonders upon Pharaoh — the founding evidence of the LORD's redeeming power.
Then thou shewedst me their doings — private disclosure of hidden danger to a threatened prophet.
So didst thou get thee a name, as it is this day — the lasting testimony that disclosure leaves behind.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of ANOINT)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of anoint, from Old French enoint, from Latin inunguere (to smear on), formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar, and where thou vowedst a vow unto me.

Anointedst appears once in the Authorized Version, in the LORD's own words to Jacob, recalling a specific act Jacob himself had performed twenty years earlier at Bethel — setting up a stone pillar and pouring oil upon it after his dream of the ladder reaching to heaven. What makes the verse remarkable is its speaker: this is not a narrator's report of what Jacob did but God's own recollection of it, spoken to summon Jacob back to obedience after two decades in Laban's household. The LORD identifies Himself by that very memory — I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar — binding His own self-disclosure to the moment Jacob marked with oil and vow. Anointedst here names not priestly consecration but a personal, spontaneous act of worship, a stone set apart in response to a vision, sealed with a vow the LORD now calls Jacob to remember and fulfil. The word stands as evidence that God keeps count of small acts of worship offered long before, and returns to them as grounds for present obedience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ANOINT: to pour oil upon; to consecrate by unction; here in the archaic second-person singular past, anointedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: ANOINT, v.t. To pour oil upon; to smear or rub over with oil.
ANOINT, v.t. To consecrate by unction, or the use of oil.
ANOINT, v.t. To set apart to a sacred use or office.
ANOINTEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as vowedst.
In Genesis 31:13 the word names Jacob's own act at Bethel, recalled by God Himself as grounds for present obedience.
scriptures: I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar, and where thou vowedst a vow unto me: now arise, get thee out from this land, and return unto the land of thy kindred.
corruption_summary: A reading that treats Genesis 31:13 as background detail misses that the verse turns on God's own memory of a private act of worship, a striking testimony against any view that small, unwitnessed devotion goes unnoticed or unused by providence.
corruption_paragraphs: A minimizing reading can pass over anointedst as incidental scene-setting for the real business of the verse, the command to return home; but the LORD's self-identification is built entirely on that earlier act — He does not say merely 'I am the LORD' but I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar, making Jacob's own worship the very ground of the present word.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a vow and an anointing made in solitude twenty years earlier were remembered by God and returned to as the basis of a fresh command — small acts of worship are not lost to providence.
roots_summary: Anointedst occurs once, in God's own recollection of Jacob's pillar at Bethel, tying a private act of worship made decades earlier directly to a present command to return and obey.
roots_lines: Anointedst in Genesis 31:13 recalls Jacob's pillar and vow at Bethel from Genesis 28.
The LORD identifies Himself by this memory: 'I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst.'
The vow Jacob made at that anointing is now called back into force as grounds for obedience.
Jacob's response is immediate: he gathers his household and flees Laban's country toward Canaan.
The pillar at Bethel becomes, in Genesis 35, the site of a second anointing and covenant renewal.
usage: Where thou anointedst the pillar — a private act of worship remembered by God decades later.
And where thou vowedst a vow unto me — the anointing bound to a promise now called due.
Now arise, get thee out from this land — present obedience grounded in past devotion.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of FILL)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of fill, from Old English fyllan, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not... thou filledst many people.

Filledst appears twice in the Authorized Version, and the two occurrences run in opposite directions. Deuteronomy 6:11 uses filledst to name what Israel did NOT do — houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not — part of Moses' catalogue of unearned inheritance warning the people against forgetting the true source of their plenty. Ezekiel 27:33 uses the same verb to describe what Tyre DID do, in the opposite sense: a great trading city whose wares, going forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people, enriching the kings of the earth through the sheer volume of her merchandise. Set side by side, the two occurrences frame filledst as a verb that can describe either grace received (houses filled by God, not by the recipient's own labour) or commerce achieved (a city's wares filling many peoples through its own trading skill) — and the surrounding chapters make plain which the Authorized Version commends. Deuteronomy 6 warns against forgetting the Giver; Ezekiel 27 laments a filling that will end, within a chapter, in Tyre's sudden and total shipwreck.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FILL: to make full; to supply fully; to satisfy; here in the archaic second-person singular past, filledst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: FILL, v.t. To make full; to supply with as much as can be contained.
FILL, v.t. To satisfy; to content.
FILL, v.t. To supply abundantly, as with goods or wealth.
FILLEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as plantedst.
In Deuteronomy 6:11 the word names houses filled by God, not by Israel's own labour; in Ezekiel 27:33 it names Tyre's trading wealth, filling many peoples through commerce.
scriptures: Deu 6:11
And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;
When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise.
corruption_summary: A reading that takes filledst as praise of prosperity wherever it appears misses that the Authorized Version uses the very same verb to commend unearned grace in Deuteronomy and to lament self-made commercial glory in Ezekiel, a glory the chapter goes on to sink without warning.
corruption_paragraphs: A prosperity-minded reading might lift Ezekiel 27's filledst many people as a picture of blessed abundance, missing that the whole chapter is a funeral dirge over Tyre, whose filling of the nations with her merchandise is precisely the greatness that collapses into sudden ruin in the verses immediately following.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that filledst names two different fillings and the text plainly favours one over the other: the houses Israel did not fill for themselves are the model of grace to be remembered gratefully, while the wealth Tyre filled the nations with by her own trade is the model of self-made glory the prophets everywhere warn will not last.
roots_summary: Filledst occurs twice, once naming grace received without labour in Deuteronomy and once naming commercial wealth achieved through trade in Ezekiel's dirge over Tyre, the two uses framing a contrast the Authorized Version does not leave the reader to guess at.
roots_lines: Filledst in Deuteronomy 6:11 names houses full of good things Israel did not labour to fill.
The verse pairs filledst with diggedst and plantedst, all naming unearned inheritance.
Filledst in Ezekiel 27:33 names Tyre's wares filling many peoples through maritime trade.
The very next verses of Ezekiel 27 picture that same Tyre suddenly shipwrecked and mourned.
The contrast is deliberate: one filling is grace to be remembered, the other pride about to fall.
usage: Houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not — grace received without labour.
Thou filledst many people — Tyre's wealth spread abroad through trade, on the eve of ruin.
The same verb names two fillings, and the text plainly favours the one given, not the one made.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of FORSAKE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of forsake, from Old English forsacan (to deny, refuse, renounce), formed with the -est ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness.

Forsookest appears once in the Authorized Version, in Nehemiah's great communal prayer of confession, and its single occurrence is a negative — the whole force of the verse is that God forsookest them NOT. The prayer has just finished cataloguing Israel's wilderness rebellions in unsparing detail: a molten calf, refusal to enter the land, hardened necks, appointment of a captain to return to bondage. Against that record of provoked patience, forsookest them not stands as the pivot of the entire confession, the mercy that makes possible everything the prayer will go on to say. The pillar of cloud did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night — the guiding presence remained precisely because the forsaking that Israel's conduct had earned did not come. This is covenant faithfulness defined by its opposite: not a description of what God did, but of the abandonment His manifold mercies refused to permit, even when Israel's own record gave ample grounds for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FORSAKE: to abandon; to desert; to renounce entirely; here in the archaic second-person singular past, forsookest, addressed to thou.
webster_full: FORSAKE, v.t. To desert; to leave utterly; to abandon.
FORSAKE, v.t. To renounce; to reject entirely.
FORSAKE, v.t. To fail; to leave without help or support.
FORSOOKEST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -est, as knewest.
In Nehemiah 9:19 the word appears in the negative, forsookest them not, naming the mercy that outlasted repeated rebellion.
scriptures: Neh 9:19

Yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness: the pillar of the cloud departed not from them by day, to lead them in the way; neither the pillar of fire by night, to shew them light, and the way wherein they should go.
corruption_summary: A reading that skims Nehemiah's confession for its list of Israel's sins can miss that the prayer's actual centre of gravity is the negative verb forsookest them not — the mercy withheld from a people whose own record gave every ground for abandonment.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading focused only on the wilderness generation's rebellions can treat forsookest them not as a mild aside rather than the hinge of the whole confession; Nehemiah 9 is structured precisely to make this verse the turn, moving from an unsparing catalogue of provocation to the single fact of mercy that explains why any of Israel's later history exists at all.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that forsookest them not is covenant faithfulness named by its refusal — the pillar of cloud and fire remained not because Israel had earned continued presence but because manifold mercies overruled a record that would otherwise have justified abandonment.
roots_summary: Forsookest occurs once, at the pivot of Nehemiah's national prayer of confession, turning from a catalogue of wilderness rebellion to the single mercy that explains Israel's continued existence.
roots_lines: Forsookest appears only in the negative: 'forsookest them not,' Nehemiah 9:19.
The verse follows immediately after a list of the golden calf, refusal to enter Canaan, and hardened necks.
The pillar of cloud and pillar of fire are named as the visible form the non-forsaking took.
Nehemiah 9 as a whole moves from confession of sin to praise of preserved mercy.
The prayer closes with a fresh covenant sealed by the returned remnant, grounded in this same mercy.
usage: Thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not — the pivot of the whole confession.
The pillar of the cloud departed not from them by day — mercy made visible in guidance.
Neither the pillar of fire by night — the same mercy extended through every watch.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of TAKE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of take, from Old Norse taka, formed with the -est ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
And tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them.

Tookest appears once in the Authorized Version, in Ezekiel's second great oracle of covenant unfaithfulness, addressed to Jerusalem under the figure of Aholibah. The verse sits inside a detailed inventory of betrayal: garments the LORD had given for covenant use are tookest and coveredst — that is, taken and used to adorn idols and impress foreign lovers rather than kept for their intended purpose. The specificity is deliberate. Ezekiel does not accuse Jerusalem in the abstract; he itemizes exactly what was taken and how it was misused, garment by garment, in a chapter built entirely from such itemized charges. Tookest names an act that in itself is neutral — taking one's own broidered garments — but which becomes the very picture of unfaithfulness once the object and purpose of the taking are named: not modest use before the LORD, but display before rivals. The word stands as one link in a long chain of similarly itemized verbs (deckedst, paintedst, playedst) that together build Ezekiel's case that Jerusalem's sin was neither vague nor accidental but detailed and deliberate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TAKE: to lay hold of; to seize; to receive; here in the archaic second-person singular past, tookest, addressed to thou.
webster_full: TAKE, v.t. To lay hold of; to seize; to grasp.
TAKE, v.t. To receive what is offered or given.
TAKE, v.t. To use, employ, or appropriate to a purpose.
TOOKEST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -est, as gavest.
In Ezekiel 16:18 the word names garments taken from their intended covenant use and turned to idolatrous display.
scriptures: And tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them: and thou hast set mine oil and mine incense before them.
corruption_summary: A reading that treats tookest as an incidental verb in an otherwise vivid chapter misses that Ezekiel 16's whole indictment is built from exactly such itemized, specific acts, each one naming a gift redirected from covenant use to rival worship.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading eager to move past the chapter's uncomfortable imagery can pass over tookest as mere narrative colour, missing that the specificity is the argument — this is not a general charge of unfaithfulness but a bill of particulars, garments tookest and coveredst upon idols, oil and incense set before them that were meant for the LORD alone.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that tookest names an ordinary, even lawful action (taking one's own garments) that becomes sin entirely through its redirected object and purpose — the same lesson Scripture presses elsewhere, that gifts are judged by their use, not merely their possession.
roots_summary: Tookest occurs once, inside Ezekiel's itemized indictment of Jerusalem's idolatry, naming garments taken from covenant use and given instead to idols alongside oil and incense.
roots_lines: Tookest in Ezekiel 16:18 names broidered garments taken and set upon idols.
The same verse names oil and incense, covenant gifts, set before those same idols.
The chapter's itemized charges (deckedst, paintedst, tookest) build a single sustained indictment.
Ezekiel 16 opens by recounting the LORD's own gifts of clothing and adorning to Jerusalem.
The chapter closes, despite the indictment, with a promise of an everlasting covenant.
usage: Tookest thy broidered garments — covenant gifts taken up for a purpose never intended.
And coveredst them — the garments used to clothe idols rather than serve the LORD.
Thou hast set mine oil and mine incense before them — worship diverted, not merely withheld.

etymology: Comparative degree of smooth, from Old English smoth, used twice in the Authorized Version to describe deceptive speech that conceals hostile intent.
biblical_def:
The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart... her mouth is smoother than oil.

Smoother appears twice in the Authorized Version, and both occurrences use the comparative to expose a gap between speech and reality. Psalm 55:21 describes a former friend turned enemy, David's own familiar companion, whose words were smoother than butter even as war was in his heart — the comparative measuring not mere pleasantness but a deliberate softness calculated to disarm. Proverbs 5:3 applies the same figure to the strange woman's seduction: her lips drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil, the comparative again marking speech engineered to lower guard rather than to inform. In both verses smoother is not a compliment; it is a warning label. The word teaches readers of the Authorized Version to distrust speech precisely in proportion to its excessive pleasantness when the speaker's true intent is hidden — the smoother the words, both texts suggest, the more reason for the hearer to examine what lies beneath them rather than to be lulled by them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SMOOTH: even; not rough; here in the comparative, smoother, describing speech more deceptively pleasant than its speaker's true intent.
webster_full: SMOOTH, adj. Having an even surface; not rough.
SMOOTH, adj. Bland; flattering; suave in address; used often of soft or deceitful speech.
SMOOTHER, the comparative degree, more smooth.
In Psalm 55:21 the word describes a companion's flattering words masking hostile intent.
In Proverbs 5:3 the word describes the seductive speech of the strange woman.
scriptures: The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.
Pro 5:3
For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil:
corruption_summary: A reading that treats 'smoother' as neutral description of pleasant speech misses that both occurrences use the comparative as a warning, teaching that unusually pleasant words concealing hostile or seductive intent are a recognizable biblical category, not a modern cynicism.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern ear can hear 'smoother than butter' or 'smoother than oil' as simple compliments, missing that both verses supply their own interpretation in the very same breath — 'but war was in his heart,' and the chapter surrounding Proverbs 5:3 warning that her end is bitter as wormwood. The comparative is doing diagnostic work, not merely descriptive work.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is one Scripture states outright in both texts: smoothness of speech is not evidence of a smooth heart, and the wise reader is taught by these two verses to weigh words against the war or the wormwood they may be concealing.
roots_summary: Smoother occurs twice, both times as a comparative marking speech more pleasant than its speaker's true intent, once of a treacherous friend and once of the seductress of Proverbs.
roots_lines: Smoother in Psalm 55:21 describes a familiar friend's words masking a heart at war.
The same verse pairs smoother than butter with softer than oil, yet 'drawn swords.'
Smoother in Proverbs 5:3 describes the strange woman's seductive speech.
Proverbs 5 immediately warns that her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.
Both occurrences teach the same lesson: excessive verbal smoothness warrants suspicion, not comfort.
usage: The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart — flattery masking treachery.
Her mouth is smoother than oil — seduction dressed as sweetness.
Both verses supply their own warning in the same breath the smoothness is described.

pos: v. (past tense, of the archaic verb to hit, meaning to strike or reach a mark)
etymology: From Old Norse hitta (to meet with, to light upon), an ordinary verb of striking or reaching a mark, appearing twice in the Authorized Version in the identical account of Saul's last battle.
biblical_def:
And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him.

Hit appears twice in the Authorized Version, in the two parallel accounts (1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles) of King Saul's final battle on Mount Gilboa. Both times the verb describes the same event from the same angle: the archers hit him, the arrows finding their mark on the doomed king even as the battle went sore against Israel on every side. The plainness of the word suits the plainness of the moment — this is not an oracle or a poem but a battlefield report, and hit does the ordinary work of naming a decisive strike without any figurative weight. What gives the verse its force is context rather than vocabulary: this is the same Saul once anointed and exalted, now struck down by enemy archers in the very land the LORD had given Israel, his end fulfilling the doom Samuel had pronounced years earlier. The marginal reading (found him) confirms the sense — the arrows sought their target and did not miss. Hit, in both occurrences, marks the moment a long-declining reign reaches its end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HIT: to strike; to touch with a blow; to reach the mark aimed at; here in the simple past, describing arrows finding their mark.
webster_full: HIT, v.t. To strike; to touch or reach with a blow, missile, or stroke.
HIT, v.t. To reach the mark aimed at; to succeed in striking.
HIT, v.i. To come or light upon, as by chance or effort.
The past tense, hit, is identical in form to the present, an irregular English verb.
In 1 Samuel 31:3 and 1 Chronicles 10:3 the word names the archers' arrows finding King Saul.
scriptures: And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers.
And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was wounded of the archers.
corruption_summary: There is no live postmodern redefinition of this plain battlefield verb; the entry exists to note that even the Bible's most ordinary vocabulary carries real weight when it names the moment a reign ends.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hit is among the plainest verbs in the Authorized Version, retaining across four centuries the same sense it has today.

The principle to recover is not a corrected meaning but a right reading of what plain narrative vocabulary is doing: the double record of the archers hit him, repeated nearly word for word in Samuel and Chronicles, marks the certainty and finality of Saul's judgment without any figurative dressing — sometimes the plainest word carries the heaviest event.
roots_summary: Hit occurs twice, in the parallel Samuel and Chronicles accounts of Saul's death on Gilboa, the identical wording in both books underscoring the certainty of the king's end.
roots_lines: Hit in 1 Samuel 31:3 names the archers' arrows finding King Saul in his last battle.
1 Chronicles 10:3 repeats the same verse almost verbatim, confirming the same event.
The marginal reading 'Heb. found him' reinforces that the arrows did not miss their mark.
Saul's death by these arrows fulfills the doom Samuel pronounced in 1 Samuel 28.
The battle of Gilboa also claims the lives of Saul's three sons, including Jonathan.
usage: And the archers hit him — the arrows finding their mark in the king's final battle.
He was sore wounded of the archers — the plain result of a plain verb.
The same sentence, repeated in Samuel and Chronicles, seals the certainty of Saul's end.

etymology: Archaic form of ago, from Old English agan (past participle of agan, to pass away), the older full form from which ago is a worn-down survival; appearing once in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
My master left me, because three days agone I fell sick.

Agone appears once in the Authorized Version, in the mouth of an unnamed Egyptian servant found starving in the field, abandoned by his Amalekite master after falling ill. The word is simply the fuller, older form of ago, and the man uses it to answer David's question about how long he has gone without food or water: three days agone. The moment is small but consequential — this servant, cast off by his own master for the crime of sickness, becomes in the next verses the very man who guides David to the Amalekite raiding camp, enabling David to recover the wives, children, and goods of Ziklag that had been carried away. Agone marks the precise measure of his abandonment (three days) that in turn becomes the measure of David's mercy: David feeds him, revives him, and in exchange receives the intelligence that leads to total recovery of everything lost. The word itself is unremarkable, but the sentence it completes turns an act of cruelty (abandonment for sickness) into the hinge of a whole chapter's deliverance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from AGONE: gone by; past; the fuller archaic form of ago, of which ago is a contraction.
webster_full: AGONE, adv. Ago; past; gone by, as time.
AGONE is the older, fuller form; AGO is its worn-down survival in later English.
Both forms measure elapsed time from the moment of speaking.
AGONE appears once in the Authorized Version, in the speech of a rescued Egyptian servant.
In 1 Samuel 30:13 the word measures the three days since the servant was abandoned and fell sick.
scriptures: And David said unto him, To whom belongest thou? and whence art thou? And he said, I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite; and my master left me, because three days agone I fell sick.
corruption_summary: There is no live postmodern redefinition of this ordinary archaic adverb; the entry exists to note that a single small word of measured time becomes, in its narrative context, the hinge of a whole chapter of deliverance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Agone is simply the older form of ago, retaining the same sense across the centuries.

The principle to recover is not a corrected meaning but a right reading of what a small measured detail accomplishes in narrative: 'three days agone' fixes the exact span of the servant's abandonment, and that precise span becomes, within a few verses, the very information that lets David overtake the Amalekites and recover everything Ziklag had lost — an ordinary word of time-telling doing weighty narrative work.
roots_summary: Agone occurs once, in the mouth of the abandoned Egyptian servant whose rescue by David leads directly to the recovery of Ziklag's captives and goods.
roots_lines: Agone in 1 Samuel 30:13 measures the three days since the servant's master abandoned him.
The servant was left to die because he fell sick, a small cruelty within a larger raid.
David feeds and revives the servant before asking anything further of him.
The servant's knowledge of the Amalekite camp becomes the key to David's pursuit.
The chapter ends with David recovering all that was taken, losing nothing.
usage: Three days agone I fell sick — the exact measure of an abandonment about to be reversed.
My master left me — cruelty answered, a few verses later, by David's mercy.
The small detail of time becomes the key that unlocks the whole chapter's deliverance.
